strengths: The principal contribution is a useful task and benchmark combining sound-conditioned segmentation with persistent instance identities. AVISeg provides 94,074 masks across 926 videos, averaging 61.4 seconds, with 26 categories and substantial multi-source content. This meaningfully extends the evaluation supported by binary and semantic audio-visual segmentation datasets.

The supervised results support the baseline's effectiveness independently of the proposed FSLA metric. Under the stated shared ResNet-50 and training schedule, AVISM achieves 61.73 HOTA and 40.57 mAP versus COMBO's 57.39 and 37.84 (Table 2). Adding video-level fusion improves the frame-fusion baseline from 59.59 to 61.73 HOTA and from 39.06 to 40.57 mAP (Table 4).

AVISM is a technically coherent adaptation of Mask2Former and VITA. Compressing frames into object tokens and applying temporal audio-visual attention provides a reasonable baseline for longer sequences. Window-size and pretraining ablations offer useful evidence about its design.

The task illustrations, architecture diagrams, supplementary implementation details, and explicit failure cases make the work understandable. Overall, the benchmark contribution and improvements under established metrics provide a stronger case for acceptance, despite meaningful evaluation and reproducibility reservations.
weaknesses: The FSLA specification has substantive inconsistencies. Algorithm 1 counts silent frames as correct without checking predictions, omits the stated object-count and category checks, and initializes counters outside the IoU-threshold loop without resetting them. The prose specifies class averaging, whereas the algorithm averages frames. Consequently, the reported FSLA results cannot be reproduced from the supplied procedure. These discrepancies do not establish that the separate HOTA and mAP results are incorrect.

Annotation reliability is insufficiently characterized for the benchmark's central difficulty. Section 4 describes SAM-assisted masks and repeated manual review, but provides neither agreement measurements nor precise rules for ambiguous sound attribution and identity continuity through silent intervals. Accurate mask boundaries alone do not establish that the correct individual source was labeled in mixtures of similar sounds.

The broad conclusions about multimodal large models exceed the evidence from their adaptations. Sections 11.1–11.4 explicitly associate masks by category or treat each category as one instance; Sam4AVS additionally selects only the top audio category. These choices structurally restrict multi-instance performance. Table 3 therefore characterizes the specified pipelines, with limited ability to isolate the underlying models' instance reasoning capabilities.

Evidence for the motivating same-category and long-range association challenges remains limited. FSLAm combines different kinds of multi-source scenes, without a dedicated same-category breakdown, although Figure 10 identifies these as important failures. Evaluation at 1 FPS and the maximum-frame capacity measurements in Table 5 also leave performance across long silent gaps and increasing sequence lengths unresolved.

Reproducibility needs further documentation. Although Section 10 supplies several useful settings, training clip sampling and the depth of the new fusion module remain unspecified, and the manuscript provides no dataset or evaluation-code access location. These are correctable reporting gaps, but they matter particularly for independently implementing the new benchmark.
